div.p: Among the many and various errors of those who live recklessly and without reflection, I could name almost nothing, my excellent Liberalis, more unworthy than this: that we do not know how either to give or to receive benefits. For it follows that, being ill placed, they are ill repaid; and when they are not returned, we complain too late, since they were already lost at the moment of giving. Nor is it any wonder that, among our many and our greatest vices, none is more common than ingratitude. 1.2 This, I see, comes about from several causes. The first is that we do not choose worthy persons on whom to bestow our gifts. When we are about to lend money at interest, we inquire carefully into the estate and the habits of the debtor; we do not scatter seed on exhausted and barren ground; yet our benefits we fling out with no discrimination at all, rather than bestow them. 1.3 And I could not easily say which is the more shameful: to disown a benefit, or to ask its return. For this is the kind of debt from which only so much is to be recovered as is repaid of the debtor's own accord. To default on it is utterly base, and for this very reason: that to discharge our faith we need not means but only the will, since he who owns the debt has repaid the benefit. But while the fault lies with those who are not grateful even by confession, it lies with us as well. 1.4 We find many men ungrateful; we make more so, because at one time we are harsh in our reproaches and our demands, at another fickle and quick to repent of our gift, at another querulous and quibbling over the smallest details. We corrupt all gratitude, not only after we have given our benefits, but in the very act of giving. 1.5 Which of us has ever been content to be asked once, or lightly? Who, when he suspected that something was being sought of him, has not knit his brow, turned away his face, feigned engagements, by long-winded talk deliberately brought to no conclusion robbed the other of his chance to ask, and by various devices baffled the pressing need; 1.6 and, when cornered in a tight place, either put the matter off, that is, gave a timid refusal, or else promised, but grudgingly, with frowning brows, with grudging words that scarcely passed his lips? 1.7 Yet no one willingly owes what he did not receive but extorted. Can anyone be grateful toward a man who flung his benefit at him in arrogance, or hurled it in anger, or gave it out of weariness, merely to be rid of the nuisance? He is mistaken who hopes for a return from one whom he has worn out by delay and tortured by suspense. 1.8 A benefit is repaid in the same spirit in which it is given, and for that reason it should not be given carelessly; for each man owes the debt to himself when he has received it from one who did not know he gave. Nor should it be given slowly, since in every act of service the giver's will is rated highly, and he who acted slowly was for a long time unwilling. Above all, it should not be given insultingly; for since nature has so arranged us that injuries sink deeper than kindnesses, and that the latter quickly slip away while a tenacious memory keeps guard over the former, what can he expect who gives offense in the very act of laying us under obligation? Toward such a man one is grateful enough if one merely forgives him his benefit. 1.9 But there is no reason why the multitude of the ungrateful should make us slower to do good. For, in the first place, as I have said, it is we who swell their number; and, in the second place, not even the immortal gods are deterred from their lavish and unceasing bounty by men who are sacrilegious and neglectful of them. They follow their own nature, and they help all things, even those very men who misjudge their gifts. Let us follow these as our guides, so far as human frailty allows; let us bestow benefits, not lend them out at interest. He deserves to be cheated who, when he gave, was thinking of repayment. "But it turned out badly." 1.10 Children and wives, too, have disappointed our hopes; yet we still rear the one and marry the other, and we are so stubborn in the face of experience that, beaten in war, we go back to war, and shipwrecked, we go back to the sea. How much more fitting it is to persevere in giving benefits! For if a man does not give because he has not received a return, he gave in order to receive, and he furnishes the ungrateful with a good excuse, men for whom it is shameful not to repay only if they may. 1.11 How many are unworthy of the light! Yet the day still dawns. How many complain that they were ever born! Yet Nature still begets new offspring, and suffers even those to exist who would rather never have been. 1.12 It is the mark of a great and good soul to pursue, not the fruits of its benefits, but the benefits themselves, and to seek the good man even after meeting bad ones. What would be magnificent in helping the many, if no one ever cheated us? As it is, it is a virtue to bestow benefits that will surely never be returned, the fruit of which has already been gathered, at once, by the man of true worth. 1.13 So far, indeed, should this thing not put us to flight and make us more sluggish toward the fairest of all undertakings, that, were I cut off from all hope of finding a grateful man, I would rather not receive benefits than not give them; for he who does not give anticipates the fault of the ungrateful. I will say what I think: he who does not repay a benefit sins the more; he who does not give it sins the sooner. 2.1 "When you have set out to lavish benefits upon the crowd, many must be lost so that you may once place one well." In the first line you may find fault on two counts: for benefits should not be poured out upon the crowd, and the lavishing of anything, least of all of benefits, is never honorable; for if you take judgment away from them, they cease to be benefits and fall under any other name you please. 2.2 The following thought is admirable, that one benefit well placed consoles us for the loss of many. But see, I beg you, whether this be not both truer and better suited to the greatness of the benefactor: that we should urge him to give even though he is destined to place none well. For that other saying is false, "many must be lost"; not one is lost, since he who loses it had reckoned the cost beforehand. 2.3 The accounting of benefits is simple: so much is paid out; if any is returned, it is gain; if none is returned, there is no loss. I gave it in order to give. No one enters his benefits in a ledger, nor, like a grasping creditor, calls them in to the hour and the day. The good man never thinks of them unless reminded by the one who repays; otherwise they pass into the form of a loan. To enter a benefit as an expense is base usury. 2.4 Whatever the outcome of your earlier gifts, persevere in bestowing them on others; they will lie better with the ungrateful, whom shame, or occasion, or imitation may one day make grateful. Do not slacken; carry through your work and play the part of the good man. Help one with money, another with credit, another with influence, another with counsel, another with wholesome precepts. 2.5 Even wild beasts feel kindnesses, nor is there any creature so savage that care does not tame it and turn it to love its keeper. The mouths of lions are handled with impunity by their trainers; the ferocity of elephants is won over to slavish obedience by food. So true is it that, even in things set beyond the understanding and appreciation of a benefit, the persistence of unflagging kindness nonetheless prevails. Is a man ungrateful for one benefit? He will not be so for a second. Has he forgotten two? A third will bring back to his memory even those that had slipped away. 3.1 That man will lose his benefits who is too quick to believe he has lost them; but he who presses on, and heaps new ones upon the old, draws out gratitude even from a hard and forgetful heart. The ungrateful man will not dare to lift his eyes against so many; wherever he turns, fleeing his own memory, let him see you there. Hem him in with your benefits. 3.2 What the force and the property of these things may be I shall tell, if first you will allow me to leap past those matters that do not bear upon our subject: why the Graces are three in number, and why they are sisters, and why with hands interlinked, and why smiling, and young, and maidens, and clad in loose and transparent robes. 3.3 Some, indeed, would have it that the one represents the bestowing of a benefit, the second the receiving of it, and the third the returning of it; others hold that there are three kinds of benefactors: those who earn benefits, those who return them, and those who at once receive and return them. 3.4 But judge either of these accounts true, what does such knowledge profit us? What does that ring of figures mean, dancing back upon itself with linked hands? This: that the course of a benefit passing from hand to hand nonetheless returns to the giver, and loses the beauty of the whole if it is ever broken, but is most beautiful if it holds together and keeps its turns unbroken. Yet within it there is some greater dignity, as in those who first earn our thanks. 3.5 Their faces are cheerful, as those of men who give or receive benefits are wont to be; they are young, because the memory of benefits ought not to grow old; they are maidens, because benefits are uncorrupted and sincere and held sacred by all, in which it is fitting that there be nothing binding or constraining; therefore they wear ungirded tunics, and these transparent, because benefits desire to be seen. 3.6 Let there be someone so enslaved to the Greeks as to call all this essential; yet there will be no one who judges that even this bears upon our subject: what names Hesiod bestowed upon them. He called the eldest Aglaia, the middle one Euphrosyne, the third Thalia. The interpretation of these names each man bends as he sees fit, and tries to lead them round to some principle, although Hesiod gave his maidens whatever name he pleased. 3.7 And so Homer changed the name of one, called her Pasithea, and promised her in marriage, that you may know they are not Vestal virgins. I shall find another poet in whom they go girt, and come forth in close-woven robes, or in robes of Phrygian wool. Mercury, too, stands with them, not because reason or eloquence commends benefits, but because the painter thought fit. 3.8 Chrysippus also, who possesses that subtle keenness which pierces to the inmost truth, who speaks for the sake of action and uses words no further than is enough for understanding, fills his whole book with these trifles, so that he says very little about the actual duty of giving, of receiving, and of returning a benefit; nor does he insert these fables into his subject, but his subject into the fables. 3.9 For, besides what Hecaton copies down, Chrysippus says that the three Graces are the daughters of Jupiter and Eurynome, younger in age than the Hours, but somewhat fairer of face, and for that reason given to Venus as her companions. He judges that the mother's name, too, bears upon the matter: that she was called Eurynome because to distribute benefits belongs to one of a widely extending estate, as though a mother were usually named after her daughters, or as though poets gave true names! 3.10 Just as audacity serves a nomenclator in place of memory, and to anyone whose name he cannot supply he assigns one, so poets think it has no bearing on their purpose to tell the truth, but, either compelled by necessity or corrupted by elegance, they bid each be called whatever falls neatly into the verse. Nor is it held against them if they have entered another name on the roll; for the next poet bids the Graces bear his own name. That you may know this is so, behold Thalia, who is precisely our subject here: in Hesiod she is one of the Graces, in Homer one of the Muses. 4.1 But, that I may not do the very thing I blame, I shall leave aside all these matters which are so far outside the subject as not even to lie near it. Only do you protect me if anyone reproaches me for having put Chrysippus in his place, a great man, by Hercules, but a Greek for all that, whose keenness, too finely whetted, is blunted and often turns back upon itself; even when he seems to be doing something, he pricks, he does not pierce through. But here what keenness is there? 4.2 We have to speak of benefits and to set in order a matter that more than any other binds human society together; we must lay down a law for life, lest under the appearance of kindness a heedless readiness should win our favor, lest this very vigilance should restrain liberality, which ought neither to be lacking nor to overflow, even while it tempers it; 4.3 men must be taught to give gladly, to receive gladly, to return gladly, and to set themselves a great contest, namely to surpass, and not merely to match, in deed and in spirit, those to whom they are bound, since he who owes a return of gratitude never overtakes the other unless he has outrun him; these must be taught to charge nothing to account, those to count themselves the deeper in debt. 4.4 To this most honorable contest of conquering benefits with benefits Chrysippus thus exhorts us: by saying that we must beware lest, since the Graces are the daughters of Jupiter, to behave ungratefully be a sacrilege and an injury done to such pretty maidens! 4.5 Do you teach me something of those things by which I may become more bountiful and more grateful toward those who deserve well of me, by which the souls of those who lay men under obligation and of those who are laid under it may strive together, so that they who have bestowed may forget, and the memory of those who owe may be tenacious. As for these trifles, let them be left to the poets, whose aim is to charm the ear and to weave a pleasing tale. 4.6 But those who wish to heal men's characters, to maintain good faith in human affairs, and to fix the memory of services in their souls, let them speak in earnest and act with all their might; unless, perhaps, you think that by light and fabulous talk, by old wives' arguments, the most ruinous of all things can be checked, the cancellation of the debts of benefits. 5.1 But, as I shall hurry past what is superfluous, so I must set forth that this is the first thing we have to learn: what we owe when we have received a benefit. For one man says that he owes the money he received, another a consulship, another a priesthood, another a province. 5.2 But these are the tokens of services, not the services themselves. A benefit cannot be touched by the hand; the matter is transacted in the mind. There is a great difference between the material of a benefit and the benefit itself; and therefore neither gold nor silver nor any of the things that are taken to be the greatest is a benefit, but the very will of the giver. The ignorant, however, mark only that which strikes the eye, which is handed over and possessed, while they set little store by that which in the transaction is precious and of price. 5.3 These things that we hold, that we gaze upon, on which our greed fastens, are perishable; both fortune and wrong can take them from us. But a benefit endures even after that has been lost through which it was given; for it is a right action, which no force can render void. 5.4 I ransomed a friend from pirates; another enemy seized him and shut him up in prison; he took away, not my benefit, but the use of my benefit. I gave back to a man his children, snatched from a shipwreck or rescued from a fire; disease, or some chance wrong, has carried them off; yet that which was given in them remains even without them. 5.5 All those things, then, which usurp the false name of benefit are but the instruments through which a friendly will unfolds itself. This happens in other matters too, that the appearance of a thing is in one place, the thing itself in another. A general decorates a man with collars, with the mural and the civic crown. 5.6 What value has the crown in itself? Or the bordered robe? Or the rods? Or the tribunal and the chariot? None of these is the honor; they are the emblems of honor. So too the benefit is not that which comes before the eyes, but the trace and the mark of the benefit. 6.1 What, then, is a benefit? A kindly action which bestows joy and in bestowing takes joy, inclined and of its own accord ready for what it does. And so it is not what is done or what is given that matters, but the spirit in which it is done, since a benefit consists, not in what is done or given, but in the very mind of the giver or doer. 6.2 That there is a great distinction between these you may understand even from this, that a benefit is undoubtedly a good, whereas that which is done or given is neither good nor evil. It is the mind that exalts small things, that gives luster to mean ones, that dishonors the great and highly prized; the things themselves that are sought have neither nature, neither good nor evil; it matters in which direction the ruling power drives them, by which form is given to things. 6.3 The benefit itself is not that which is counted out or handed over, just as in the case of victims, even though they be fat and gleam with gold, it is not these that constitute the worship of the gods, but the upright and devout will of the worshipers. And so the good are devout even with meal and a handful of grain; the wicked, on the other hand, do not escape impiety, though they drench the altars with abundant blood. 7.1 If benefits consisted in things, and not in the very will to do good, they would be greater in proportion as what we receive is greater. But this is false; for sometimes the man who lays us under deeper obligation is one who gave little but with a great spirit, who "matched the wealth of kings in soul," who bestowed a trifle but gladly, who forgot his own poverty while he looked to mine, who had not merely the will to help but the eager desire, who thought that he received a benefit when he gave it, who gave as though he would never recover it, recovered it as though he had not given it, who both seized and sought the chance to be of use. 7.2 On the contrary, as I have said, those gifts are thankless, however great they may seem in substance and appearance, which are either wrung from the giver or fall from him; and that comes far more welcome which is given with a ready hand than with a full one. 7.3 "It is a trifle that he bestowed on me, but he could do no more"; whereas "what this man gave is great, but he hesitated, but he delayed, but he groaned in the giving, but he gave it haughtily, but he carried it round for show, and wished to please, not the man on whom he bestowed it, but his own ambition; it was to vanity that he gave it, not to me." 8.1 When all were offering Socrates many gifts, each according to his means, Aeschines, a poor disciple, said: "I can find nothing worthy of you that I am able to give you, and in this one respect alone do I feel myself a poor man. And so I give you the one thing I possess, myself. This gift, such as it is, I beg you to accept in good part, and to bear in mind that others, when they gave you much, left more for themselves." To him Socrates replied: 8.2 "Why, surely you have given me a great gift, unless perhaps you rate yourself cheaply? I shall therefore make it my care to give you back to yourself a better man than I received you." By this gift Aeschines surpassed the soul of Alcibiades, the equal of riches, and all the munificence of the wealthy youths. 9.1 You see how the mind finds the material of liberality even amid straitened means. Aeschines seems to me to have said: "You have accomplished nothing, Fortune, by willing me to be poor; I shall nonetheless contrive a gift worthy of this man, and since I cannot give from what is yours, I shall give from what is my own." And there is no reason to suppose that he held himself cheap: he made of himself his own price. The ingenious youth found out how to give Socrates to himself. We must look, not at how great each gift is, but from what kind of person it proceeds. 9.2 The shrewd man did not grant easy access to those whose cravings were immoderate, and, while doing nothing for them in deed, cherished their wicked hopes with words; but he is held in worse repute who, harsh of tongue and stern of face, set forth his good fortune with an air of envy. For men court and detest the prosperous, and, ready themselves to do the same things if they could, they hate the man who does them. 9.3 Wives belong to others, and are made the laughing-stock not even in secret but openly; and men hand over their own to others. He is counted a boor, an uncivilized fellow of bad manners, and among matrons an abominable sort of husband, who has forbidden his wife to be carried about for sale in a sedan and conveyed visible on every side to a crowd of admitted spectators. 9.4 If a man has made himself conspicuous by no mistress, and pays no yearly allowance to another's wife, the matrons call him a fellow of low and sordid lust, a chaser of serving-maids. Hence the most respectable form of betrothal is adultery, and widowhood passes for celibacy by common consent, since no man has married a wife unless he first led another's away. 9.5 Now men vie to scatter what they have seized, and with fierce and keen greed to gather up again what they have scattered; to count nothing of weight, to despise another's poverty and to dread their own more than any other evil, to disturb the peace with wrongs, and to crush the weaker by force and by terror. That provinces are plundered, and the court of justice put up for sale, knocked down to one of two bidders after the bidding has been heard on both sides, is no wonder, since it is the law of nations that what you have bought you may sell! 10.1 But our impetus carries us too far, the subject itself inciting us; so let us thus make an end, lest the blame settle upon our own age. This our ancestors complained of, this we complain of, this our descendants will complain of: that morals are overthrown, that wickedness reigns, that human affairs and all that is wicked are sliding into the worse. Yet these things stand and will stand in the same place, moved only a little this way or that, like the waves which a rising tide carries farther up the shore, and which, as it recedes, it holds back within the inner mark of the beach. 10.2 At one time the sin will run more to adultery than to other vices, and chastity will burst its bonds; at another the madness of banquets will flourish, and the kitchen, that foulest ruin of estates; at another there will be excessive care of the body and a concern for appearance that betrays the deformity of the soul; at another ill-governed freedom will break out into insolence and recklessness; at another men will rush into cruelty, private and public, and into the frenzy of civil wars, by which all that is holy and sacred is profaned; one day honor will be paid to drunkenness, and to have downed the most unmixed wine will be a virtue. 10.3 Vices do not wait in one place, but, restless and at variance among themselves, they are in tumult, driving one another out and being put to flight in turn; for the rest, we shall always have to pronounce the same judgment upon ourselves: that we are wicked, that we have been wicked, and, I will add it unwillingly, that we shall be wicked. 10.4 There will be murderers, tyrants, thieves, adulterers, ravishers, sacrilegious men, traitors; below all these stands the ungrateful man, except that all these spring from the ungrateful man, without whom scarcely any great crime has come to its growth. Beware lest you commit this as the greatest of crimes; pardon it as the lightest, if it has been committed against you. For this is the sum of the wrong: you have lost a benefit. The best of it remains safe for you: you gave it. 10.5 But just as we must take care to bestow our benefits above all on those who will respond gratefully, so there are some things we shall do and bestow even if we have ill hopes of the men, not only if we judge that they will be ungrateful, but if we know that they have been so. For instance, if I shall be able to restore to a man his sons, rescued from great peril at no peril of my own, I shall not hesitate. A man worthy of it I shall defend even at the cost of my own blood, and I shall enter into a share of his danger; an unworthy man, if I can snatch him from robbers by raising a shout, I shall not grudge to utter the cry that brings him safety. 11.1 It follows that we should say what benefits are to be given, and how. First let us give what is necessary, then what is useful, then what is pleasant, and above all what will endure. But we must begin with the necessary; for that which sustains life reaches the mind in one way, that which adorns or equips it in another. In the latter a man may be a fastidious appraiser, since he can easily do without it, and of it he may say: "Take it back, I do not want it; I am content with my own." Sometimes one is glad not merely to return what one received, but to fling it away. 11.2 Of the things that are necessary, some hold the first place, those without which we cannot live; some the second, those without which we ought not to live; some the third, those without which we are unwilling to live. 11.3 Of the first stamp are these: to be snatched from the hands of the enemy, from the wrath of a tyrant, from proscription, and from the other perils which, various and uncertain, beset human life. Whichever of these we have averted, the greater and the more terrible it was, the greater the gratitude we shall earn; for the thought arises of how great the evils were from which men have been freed, and the fear that went before is a foil that enhances the gift. Yet we ought not on that account to save anyone more slowly than we can, in order that fear may lend weight to our gift. 11.4 Next to these are the things without which we can indeed live, but in such a way that death would be preferable, as freedom and chastity and a sound mind. After these we shall reckon what is dear to us by ties of kinship and blood, by use and long association, such as children, wives, household gods, and all else to which the mind has so attached itself that it counts being torn from them harder than being torn from life. 11.5 Then follow useful things, of which the material is varied and wide; here will be money, not in superfluity, but provided to a sound measure of having; here will be public office and the advancement of those who aim at higher things; for nothing is more useful than to become useful to oneself. The rest comes of abundance, and is apt to make men dainty. In these we shall aim that they be welcome by their timeliness, that they be not common, but such as few have possessed, or few within this age, or in this manner, things which, even if not precious by nature, become so by their time or place. 11.6 Let us consider what gift will most delight, what will often come before the eyes of him who has it, so that as often as it is with him, so often it may be with us. Above all we shall take care not to send useless gifts: as hunting weapons to a woman or an old man, books to a peasant, nets to one devoted to study and letters. And equally, on the other side, we shall look about lest, while we wish to send what is welcome, we send what will reproach a man with his own besetting fault: as wine to a drunkard, or medicines to an invalid. For it begins to be an insult, not a gift, in which the recipient's vice is recognized. 12.1 If the choice of giving rests with us, we shall seek above all things that will endure, so that the gift may be as little subject to mortality as possible. For few men are so grateful as to think of what they have received, even when they do not see it. With the ungrateful, too, memory comes back along with the gift itself, when it is before their eyes and does not let them forget it, but thrusts and presses its author upon them. Indeed, for this very reason let us seek more lasting gifts, because we ought never to remind men; let the thing itself rouse the fading memory. 12.2 I shall more gladly give silver wrought into plate than coined; more gladly statues than clothing, and than what brief use wears away. With few does gratitude outlast the gift; with more there are men in whose minds a present lasts no longer than in use. I, if it can be done, do not wish my gift to be consumed; let it stand, let it cleave to my friend, let it live with him. 12.3 No one is so foolish as to need warning not to send anyone gladiators or a hunting show when the public spectacle is already over, or summer clothing in midwinter, winter clothing at the solstice. Let there be common sense in a benefit; let it have regard to time, to place, to persons, since certain things are welcome or unwelcome according to the moment. How much more acceptable it is if we give what a man does not have, rather than what he has in abundance; what he has long sought and not found, rather than what he is going to see everywhere! 12.4 Let gifts be not so much costly as rare and choice, such as may make a place for themselves even in a rich man's regard, just as common fruits too, and such as within a few days will pass into distaste, delight us if they have come earlier than their season. Those things, too, will not lack honor which either no one else has given to the recipients, or which we have given to no one else. 13.1 To Alexander of Macedon, when as conqueror of the East he was lifting his thoughts above the human, the Corinthians sent envoys to offer their congratulations and presented him with the citizenship of their city. When Alexander had laughed at this kind of compliment, one of the envoys said: "To no one have we ever given our citizenship save to you and to Hercules." 13.2 Gladly he accepted the undiluted honor, and, attending the envoys with an invitation and other courtesies, he reflected, not who it was that gave him their citizenship, but to whom they had given it; and the man, given over to glory, of whose nature and limit he knew nothing, following the footsteps of Hercules and of Liber, and not halting even where these had failed, looked away from the givers to the partner of his honor, as though he held the heaven which in his most empty fancy he embraced, because he was being matched with Hercules! 13.3 For what had he in common with Hercules, that frenzied youth, whose virtue was lucky recklessness? Hercules conquered nothing for himself; he passed over the world, not coveting, but judging what to conquer, the foe of the wicked, the champion of the good, the bringer of peace to land and sea. But this man, from boyhood a brigand and a ravager of nations, the bane of his enemies no less than of his friends, who counted it the highest good to be a terror to all mortals, forgot that not only the fiercest but also the most cowardly of creatures are feared for their evil venom. 14.1 Let us now return to our subject. If a man gives a benefit to anyone whatever, it is welcome to no one; no one counts himself the guest of an innkeeper or a tavern-keeper, or the table-companion of one who gives a public feast, where one may say: "What, after all, did he confer on me? Nothing but what he conferred on that man, scarcely well known to him, and even on that man, his enemy and a most base fellow. Did he, then, judge me worthy of it? He merely indulged his own disease!" Whatever you would have welcome, make rare; everyone is content to have it counted to his own credit. 14.2 Let no one so interpret these words as if I would draw liberality back and curb it with a tighter rein; let it go forth, in truth, as far as it pleases, but let it go, not stray. One may bestow gifts in such a way that each man, even though he received with many others, does not think himself one of a crowd. 14.3 Let everyone have some token of intimacy through which he may hope that he was admitted nearer. Let him say: "I received the same as that man, but unasked. I received what that man did, but I within a brief time, while he had long earned it. There are those who have the same gift, but it was not given in the same words, nor with the same kindness in the giver. That man received it after he had asked; I had not asked. That man received it, but being one who would readily repay, one whose old age and free childlessness promised much; to me he gave more, though he gave the same, because he gave without hope of return." 14.4 Just as a courtesan will so apportion herself among many that not one fails to carry away some token of an intimate regard, so let him who wishes his benefits to be loved contrive that, while many are laid under obligation, each one nonetheless has something whereby he may set himself before the rest. 15.1 I, indeed, put no obstacles in the way of benefits; the more and the greater they have been, the more praise they will bring. But let there be judgment; for things given at random and by chance can be dear to no one. 15.2 Wherefore, if anyone supposes that, in laying down these rules, we are drawing the bounds of kindness inward and opening to it a narrower path, he has misheard our admonitions. For what virtue do we revere more? To what do we apply the goad more eagerly? Or to whom does this exhortation more suit than to us who ratify the fellowship of the human race? 15.3 What, then, is the case? Since there is no honorable force of the mind, even though it begins from a right will, unless measure has made it a virtue, I forbid liberality to play the spendthrift. Then it is a joy to have received a benefit, and even with hands outstretched, when reason leads it to the worthy, and no chance or impulse, in want of counsel, carries it just anywhere, a benefit one is glad to display and to inscribe to one's own account. 15.4 Do you call those things benefits whose author one is ashamed to confess? But how much more welcome are those benefits, and how deeply they sink into the inner part of the soul, never to depart, when they delight the one who reflects more on the giver than on what he has received! 15.5 Crispus Passienus used to say that of some men he would rather have the esteem than the benefit, and of others the benefit than the esteem, and he would add examples. "I would rather have," he would say, "the esteem of the deified Augustus, the benefit of Claudius." But I, for my part, hold that no man's benefit is worth seeking whose esteem is cheap. 15.6 What, then? Was a gift not to be accepted from Claudius? It was, but as from Fortune, which you knew might at any moment turn to evil. Why do we divide these things which are mingled together? It is not a benefit which lacks its best part, namely, that it was given with judgment; otherwise a vast sum of money, if it was not given with reason and a right will, is no more a benefit than a buried treasure. There are many things, however, which one ought to accept and not to owe.

Let us examine, Liberalis, best of men, what still remains from the earlier part, namely, how a benefit is to be given; and of this I think I shall point out the most direct road: let us give as we should wish to receive. 1.2 Above all, let it be given willingly, quickly, without any hesitation. That benefit wins no thanks which has long stuck between the giver's hands, which a man has seemed loath to let go of and to give as though he were robbing himself. Even if some delay intervenes, let us avoid by all means seeming to have deliberated; for he who hesitates comes next to refusing, and earns no gratitude at all. Since in a benefit the most pleasing thing is the giver's good will, the man who by his very hanging back has borne witness that he gave unwillingly has not given, but has yielded grudgingly to one who pressed him; and yet there are many whom weakness of countenance makes liberal. 1.3 The most welcome benefits are those that are ready, easy, and come to meet us, where there has been no delay save in the modesty of the receiver. Best of all is to anticipate each man's wish; next best, to follow it. The former is better, to forestall before we are asked, since, when an honest man's lips falter at the asking and the blush comes over his face, he who spares him this torment multiplies his gift. 1.4 He has not received free of charge who received only after he had asked, since indeed, as our forefathers, men of the gravest weight, judged, nothing costs so dear as what is bought by entreaty. Men would make their vows more sparingly if they had to make them openly; so true is it that even to the gods, to whom we offer the most honorable supplication, we prefer to pray in silence and within ourselves. 2.1 It is a galling word, a heavy one, to be spoken with downcast face: "I beg." One must spare a friend this, and anyone whom you mean to make a friend by deserving well of him; let him hasten as he may, the man who gave only to the one who asked has given his benefit too late. We must therefore divine each man's wish, and, when we have grasped it, set him free from the most grievous necessity of asking; that benefit, you may be sure, will live and be welcome in his mind which came to meet him. 2.2 If we have not succeeded in forestalling him, let us cut short the asker's many words; that we may seem, not to have been asked, but to have been informed, let us promise at once, and prove by our very haste, even before we are interrupted, that we mean to act. Just as in the sick the timeliness of food is wholesome, and water given at the right moment has held the place of a remedy, so, however slight and common a benefit may be, if it was ready at hand, if it lost not one of the nearest hours, it adds much to itself and surpasses in welcome a costly gift that is slow and long pondered. He who acts with such readiness, there is no doubt, acts willingly; and so he acts gladly and wears upon his face the look of his own heart. 3.1 The huge benefits of some men have been spoiled by their silence or their slowness of speech, which counterfeited weight and gravity, since they promised with the face of men refusing. How much better to add good words to good deeds, and to commend what you bestow by kindly and humane utterance! 3.2 That the other may chide himself for having been too slow in asking, you may add a friendly complaint: "I am angry with you, because, when you wanted something, you did not wish me to know it long ago, because you asked so carefully, because you brought anyone else into it. But for my part I congratulate myself that it pleased you to put my heart to the test; hereafter, whatever you want, you shall claim by your own right; this once your awkwardness is forgiven." 3.3 Thus you will bring it about that he values your good will above that thing, whatever it was, which he had come to ask for. Then the giver's virtue is at its height, then his kindness, when he who has departed will say to himself: "I have made a great profit today; I would rather have found him such a man than that this thing, of which I spoke, had come to me multiplied by some other road; to this spirit of his I shall never be able to return an equal gratitude." 4.1 But there are very many who, by harshness of words and a haughty brow, bring their benefits into hatred, using such language and such arrogance that one repents of having obtained the favor. Then, after the thing is promised, other delays follow; and nothing is more bitter than when one has to ask even for what one has already obtained. 4.2 Benefits should be paid on the spot; yet from certain men they are harder to receive than to obtain. One man has to be asked to give the reminder, another to bring the matter to a close; thus a single gift is worn out through the hands of many, so that the least gratitude remains for him who promised it, since whoever has to be asked after him detracts from its author. 4.3 You will therefore take care, if you wish what you bestow to be reckoned with gratitude, that your benefits reach those to whom they were promised untouched, intact, without any, as they say, deduction. Let no one intercept them, let no one detain them; no one can make a favor of his own out of what you are about to give without diminishing yours. 5.1 Nothing is so bitter as long suspense; some men bear with a more even mind to have their hope cut off than dragged out. But many have this fault, that out of a perverse ambition they put off their promises, lest the throng of suitors should grow smaller, like the ministers of royal power, who delight in the long spectacle of their own pride, and judge that they can do less unless they have shown each man, long and often, what they can do. They do nothing at once, nothing at one stroke; their injuries are headlong, their benefits slow. 5.2 Hold it therefore for most true, what that comic poet said: "What? do you not understand that you take away just so much gratitude as you add of delay?" Hence those cries which honest grief wrings out: "Do it, if you are going to do anything," and: "Nothing is worth so much; I had rather you refused me at once." When the mind, worn to weariness, begins to hate the benefit while it waits for it, can it for that be grateful? 5.3 Just as the most cruel cruelty is that which drags out the punishment, and it is a kind of mercy to kill quickly, since the last torment carries with it its own end, while the time that precedes it is the largest part of the coming penalty, so the gratitude for a gift is the greater the less long it hung in suspense. For even of good things the expectation is full of anxiety; and since very many benefits bring a remedy for some distress, the man who either allows another to be tortured longer when he could free him at once, or to rejoice later, does violence to his own benefit. 5.4 All kindness hastens, and it is the mark of one who acts willingly to act quickly; he who has helped slowly, dragging it out from day to day, did not act from the heart. So he has lost the two greatest things, both the time and the proof of a friendly will; to be slow to wish is the part of one unwilling. 6.1 In every transaction, Liberalis, the manner in which a thing is said or done is no small part. Quickness adds much, delay takes away much. Just as in weapons the force of the iron is the same, but it makes an infinite difference whether they are hurled with the arm drawn back or slip from a slack hand, and the same sword both grazes and runs through, it matters with what pressure of the wrist it came, so it is the same thing that is given, but it matters how it is given. 6.2 How sweet, how precious it is, if he who gave did not suffer thanks to be rendered to him, if in the very act of giving he forgot that he had given! For to upbraid a man at the very moment you are doing him a service is madness, and to insert an insult into a kindness. And so benefits should not be made bitter, nor should anything painful be mingled with them. Even if there is something on which you wish to admonish him, choose another time. 7.1 Fabius Verrucosus used to call a benefit roughly and harshly given by a hard man "a gritty loaf," which a hungry man finds it needful to take, but bitter. 7.2 Tiberius Caesar, being asked by Marius Nepos, a man of praetorian rank, to relieve his debt, ordered him to furnish the names of his creditors; this is not to give, but to summon the creditors together. When the names had been furnished, he wrote to Nepos that he had ordered the money to be paid, adding an insulting reproof. He brought it about that Nepos neither had debt nor a benefit; he freed him from his creditors, but did not bind him to himself. Tiberius had some aim in this; 7.3 he did not wish, I suppose, that there should be many to come crowding with the same request. This may perhaps have been an effective method for repressing by shame the wicked cravings of men; but in giving a benefit a wholly different road must be followed. Everything that you give should be so adorned as to be the more welcome. But this is not to give a benefit, it is to catch a man in the act. 8.1 And, to say in passing what I think on this point too: not even for a prince is it altogether seemly to give for the sake of disgracing. "And yet," one says, "Tiberius could not even in this way escape what he was avoiding; for afterward several were found to make the same request, all of whom he ordered to give in the senate the reasons of their debt, and so gave them fixed sums." That is not liberality, it is censorship. 8.2 It is aid, it is a princely subsidy; it is not a benefit, the memory of which I cannot recall without a blush. I have been sent before a judge; to obtain my request, I had to plead my cause. 9.1 And so all the masters of wisdom prescribe that some benefits be given openly, some in secret. Openly, those which it is glorious to obtain, such as military decorations, public offices, and whatever else is made fairer by being known; 9.2 again, those which do not advance a man nor make him more honored, but succor weakness, want, or disgrace, are to be given in silence, so that they may be known to those alone whom they help. 10.1 Sometimes even the very man who is helped must be deceived, so that he may have the benefit without knowing from whom he received it. Arcesilaus, they say, judged that he should secretly help a friend who was poor and concealed his poverty, who, being ill, did not even confess this, that he lacked the means for necessary uses; without the man's knowledge he slipped a little bag of money beneath his pillow, so that one whose modesty was useless to himself might find rather than receive what he needed. 10.2 "What then? Will he not know from whom he received it?" In the first place, let him not know, if this very thing is a part of the benefit; in the second place, I shall do many other things, shall bestow many gifts, by which he may understand the author of this one too; finally, he will not know that he has received, but I shall know that I have given. "That is too little," you say. Too little, if you are thinking of lending at interest; but if of giving, you will give in the way that will most profit the receiver. You will be content to have yourself as witness; otherwise it is not the doing of good that delights you, but being seen to have done good. 10.3 "I want him by all means to know." You are looking for a debtor. "I want him by all means to know." What? if it is more useful for him not to know, if it is more honorable, more gracious, will you not turn the other way? "I want him to know." Will you then not save a man in the dark? 10.4 I do not deny that, as often as the matter allows, we should have regard to the joy that comes from the receiver's good will; but if he both needs help and is ashamed of it, if what we bestow gives offense unless it is hidden, I do not enter my benefit in the public record. Why not? I shall not be the one to declare to him that I have given, since among the first and most necessary precepts is this: never to reproach, nay, never even to remind. For this is the law of a benefit between two: the one ought at once to forget that he has given, the other never that he has received. 11.1 The frequent recalling of our services tears at the mind and oppresses it. One is moved to cry out as that man cried out who, saved in the proscription of the triumvirs by a certain friend of Caesar's, could not endure his arrogance: "Give me back to Caesar!" How long will you say: "I saved you, I snatched you from death"? That, if I remember it of my own free will, is life; if at your bidding, it is death. I owe you nothing, if you saved me only to have someone to display. How long do you parade me about? How long will you not let me forget my fortune? Once I would have been led in a triumph! We must not speak of what we have bestowed; 11.2 he who reminds asks for a return. We must not press the point, nor renew the memory, except by giving something else to recall the former gift. We ought not even to tell others of it; let him who gave the benefit be silent, let him who received it tell. For else it will be said, as was said to that man who everywhere boasted of his benefit: "You will not deny," said he, "that you have received it back"; and when the other answered, "When?" "Often indeed," said he, "and in many places, that is, as often and wherever you have told the story." 11.3 What need is there to speak out, to seize another's office? There is one who can do this more becomingly, by whose telling this too will be praised, that you do not tell it yourself. You judge me ungrateful, if no one is to know of it while you are silent! And so far is this from being permissible that, even if someone shall tell of it in our presence, we must answer: "He is indeed most worthy of greater benefits, but I know that I wish to render him all services rather than that I have so far rendered them"; and even this not in a servile fashion, nor with that figure of speech by which some men reject what they really wish to draw more toward themselves. 11.4 Then all humanity must be added. The farmer will lose what he has scattered if he abandons his labor at the seed; with much care crops are brought to the harvest; nothing comes to fruit which an even cultivation does not attend from first to last. The condition of benefits is the same. 11.5 Can there be any benefits greater than those which parents bestow on their children? Yet these are made void, if they are abandoned in infancy, unless a long devotion nourishes its gift. The condition of all other benefits is the same: unless you assist them, you will lose them; it is too little to have given, they must be cherished. If you wish to have those whom you lay under obligation grateful, you ought not only to give benefits, but to love. Above all, as I have said, let us defer to men's ears; admonition breeds weariness, reproach breeds hatred. 11.6 Nothing is so much to be avoided in giving a benefit as pride. What need of an arrogant face, what need of swelling words? The thing itself exalts you. Empty boasting must be stripped away; the deeds will speak for us while we are silent. Not only thankless, but hateful, is a benefit haughtily given. 12.1 Gaius Caesar gave Pompeius Pennus his life, if he gives who does not take it away; then, when the man had been acquitted and was rendering thanks, he held out his left foot to be kissed. Those who excuse it and deny that it was done out of insolence say that he wished to show off his gilded, nay golden, slipper, studded with pearls. Just so: what is there insulting in it, if a man of consular rank kissed gold and pearls, since there was otherwise no part of Caligula's body that he could have kissed more cleanly? 12.2 This man, born for this, to change the manners of a free state into Persian servitude, judged it too little if a senator, an old man, who had held the highest offices, had lain prostrate as a suppliant in the sight of the chief men in the very fashion in which conquered enemies have lain before their enemies; he found something below the knees by which to thrust down liberty! Is this not to trample on the commonwealth, and with the left foot at that, even though someone may think this beside the point? It was too little, then, to have been foully and madly insolent, this man who, in his slippers, sat in judgment on the life of a consular, unless the emperor had thrust his shoe-tassels into a senator's face! 13.1 O pride, the most foolish evil of great fortune! How it is a pleasure to receive nothing from you! How you turn every benefit into an injury! How everything misbecomes you! The higher you have raised yourself, the lower you are, and you show that it has not been granted you to recognize those goods with which you so puff yourself up; whatever you give, you spoil. 13.2 And so one is moved to ask why pride flings itself back so haughtily, why it distorts the look and bearing of its face, so that it would rather wear a mask than a face? Welcome are the things that are bestowed with a human countenance, at least with a gentle and calm one, which my superior gave me without exulting over me, but was as kindly as he could be and came down to my level and stripped his gift of all show, and so watched for a fitting moment that he came to my aid in opportunity rather than in dire need. 13.3 In one way only shall we persuade such men not to spoil their benefits by their insolence: if we show that benefits do not seem greater for being given with more uproar; that the men themselves cannot for that reason seem greater to anyone; that the grandeur of pride is empty, and such as brings into hatred even things that should be loved. 14.1 There are some things, harmful to those who obtain them, which it is a benefit not to give but to refuse; we shall therefore weigh the advantage rather than the wish of those who ask. For often we crave what is harmful, and we cannot discern how ruinous these things are, because passion interrupts the judgment; but when the craving has subsided, when that impulse of the burning mind, which routs counsel, has fallen, we detest the authors of harmful gifts as our undoers. 14.2 As we refuse cold water to the sick, and a sword to those who mourn and are angry with themselves, and to the mad whatever their frenzy seeks for use against themselves, so in general we shall persist in not giving what will be harmful, even to those who beg earnestly and humbly, sometimes even pitiably. It becomes us to look not only to the beginnings of our benefits but also to their ends, and to give what it will be a delight not only to receive but also to have received. There are many who say: 14.3 "I know this will not profit him, but what am I to do? He asks, I cannot resist his entreaties; let him see to it: he will complain of himself, not of me." It is false: nay, of you, and rightly too; when he has returned to a sound mind, when that fever which inflamed his spirit has abated, why should he not hate the man by whom he was helped to his own loss and peril? 14.4 To be moved by entreaties to the ruin of those who ask is a savage kindness. Just as it is a most noble work to save men even against their will and wish, so to lavish destructive things on those who beg for them is a hatred dressed up as charm and affability. Let us give a benefit which will please more and more in the using, which will never turn to evil. I shall not give money which I know is to be counted out to an adulteress, nor shall I be found a partner in a base deed or design; if I can, I shall call a man back, if not, I shall not abet his crime. 14.5 Whether anger drives him whither he ought not to go, or the heat of ambition leads him away from safety, I will not suffer him to take from me the strength for any evil, nor will I let him be able one day to say: "That man killed me by loving me." Often there is no difference between the gifts of friends and the prayers of enemies; whatever the latter wish to befall a man, to that the untimely indulgence of the former drives and equips him. And what is baser than what most frequently happens, that there is no difference between hatred and a benefit? 15.1 Let us never bestow what will redound to our own shame. Since the height of friendship is to make a friend our equal, we must take thought for both at once. I shall give to the needy, but so that I myself do not come to need; I shall succor the man about to perish, but so that I myself do not perish, unless I am to be the price of a great man or a great cause. 15.2 I shall give no benefit which it would be shameful for me to ask. I shall neither magnify a small gift, nor suffer great gifts to be received as if they were small; for as the man who charges to account what he gave destroys all gratitude, so the man who points out how much he gives commends his gift, he does not reproach with it. 15.3 Each man must have regard to his own means and powers, lest we bestow either more than we can or less. We must weigh the person to whom we give; for some things are too small to come fittingly from great men, some are too great for the receiver. Compare therefore the standing of each, and weigh between them the very thing you mean to give: whether it is too heavy or too slight for the giver, whether again the man who is to receive it will either disdain it or be unable to hold it. 16.1 Alexander was giving someone a city, that madman who could conceive nothing in his mind but the vast. When the man to whom it was being given, having taken his own measure, shrank from the ill will such a gift would bring, saying that it did not suit his fortune: "I do not ask," said Alexander, "what it becomes you to receive, but what it becomes me to give." The saying seems spirited and kingly, though it is most foolish. For nothing of itself becomes any man; it matters who gives, to whom, when, why, where, and the rest, without which the rationale of the act will not hold together. 16.2 Most swollen of creatures! If it does not become him to receive this, neither does it become you to give it; account is taken of persons and ranks, and since virtue everywhere is measure, that which exceeds errs as much as that which falls short. Granted, indeed, that this is allowed you, and that fortune has raised you so high that your largesses are cities (and how much greater of soul it had been not to take them than to scatter them!): there is nonetheless someone too small for a state to be stored away in his bosom! 17.1 A Cynic asked a talent of Antigonus; he replied that this was more than a Cynic ought to ask. Repulsed, the man asked a denarius; he replied that this was less than it became a king to give. "Most shameful is a quibble of this sort; he found a way to give neither. In the denarius he regarded the king, in the talent the Cynic, though he could have given the denarius as to a Cynic and the talent as a king. Granted that there is something too great for a Cynic to receive, nothing is so small that a king's kindness cannot honorably bestow it." 17.2 If you ask me, I approve; for it is an intolerable thing to demand money and to despise it. You have declared war on money; this you have professed, this is the part you have put on: it must be played. It is most unjust that you should acquire money under the glory of want. Each man, therefore, must look to his own person no less than to that of the man whom he is thinking of helping. 17.3 I should like to use the comparison of our own Chrysippus drawn from the game of ball, which without doubt falls either through the fault of the thrower or of the catcher; it keeps its course then, when it is fitly thrown and caught by both, passing back and forth between the hands of the two. But a good player must throw it one way to a tall partner, another to a short one. The same is the rule of a benefit. Unless it is fitted to both persons, the giver's and the receiver's, it will neither leave the one nor reach the other as it ought. 17.4 If our business is with a trained and skilled partner, we shall throw the ball more boldly; for however it comes, a ready and nimble hand will send it back; if with a beginner and an unskilled man, we shall not throw so stiffly nor with such force, but more gently, and, aiming at his very hand, shall come slack to meet it. The same must be done with benefits; let us teach some men, and judge it enough if they try, if they venture, if they are willing. 17.5 But for the most part we make men ungrateful, and encourage them to be so, as though our benefits were only then great if no gratitude could be returned for them; just as malicious players make it their object to disgrace their partner, with loss, of course, to the game itself, which cannot be prolonged unless there is mutual goodwill. 17.6 Many are of so perverse a nature that they would rather lose what they have bestowed than seem to have received it back, proud men and ledger-keepers. How much better and how much more humane to act so that these too may keep their parts, and to favor a return of gratitude to oneself, to interpret all things kindly, to listen to the man who renders thanks no otherwise than if he made a repayment, to show oneself ready for this, that one wishes even the man one has bound to be set free! 17.7 A moneylender is ill spoken of if he exacts harshly, and equally if in receiving payment he is slow and difficult and seeks pretexts for delay. A benefit is as much to be received again as not to be exacted. He is best who gave readily, never exacted, rejoiced to have it returned, in good faith forgot what he had bestowed, and received it back in the spirit of one accepting a fresh gift. 18.1 Some men not only give benefits proudly, but also receive them so, which must not be done. For let us now pass to the other part, intending to treat how men ought to bear themselves in receiving benefits. Every duty that consists of two parts demands just as much from each. When you have looked into what a father ought to be, you will know that there remains no less work there to discern what kind of man a son ought to be; there are certain parts belonging to a husband, but no smaller ones belonging to a wife. 18.2 These render in turn as much as they exact, and require a like rule, which, as Hecaton says, is difficult; for everything honorable is on a steep ascent, even what is near to the honorable; for it must not only be done, but done with reason. With this for our guide we must go through the whole of life, ordering the least and the greatest things by its counsel; we must give as it advises. And this will first judge that we should not receive from all men. From whom, then, shall we receive? To answer you briefly: from those to whom we would have given. 18.3 Let us see whether one ought to be sought with even greater discrimination to whom we are to owe than to whom we are to give. For though no disadvantages should follow (and very many do follow), it is yet a grievous torment to owe to one whom you would not; contrariwise, it is most delightful to have received a benefit from one whom you can love even after an injury, where the very cause has made the friendship, otherwise pleasant, also just. But this is most wretched to a modest and honest man, if he must love one whom he takes no pleasure in. 18.4 I must so often warn you that I am not speaking of the wise, to whom whatever is fitting is also pleasant, who have their minds in their own power and lay down for themselves what law they will, and keep the law they have laid down, but of imperfect men who wish to follow the honorable road, whose passions often obey only stubbornly. And so I must choose from whom I am to receive a benefit; 18.5 and indeed a creditor in benefits is to be sought with more care than a creditor in money. For to the latter I must pay back as much as I received, and, if I have paid, I am discharged and free; but to the former I must pay back even more, and even when the favor has been returned we still cleave together; for when I have repaid I must begin again, and the friendship abides; and as I would not admit an unworthy man into friendship, so neither into that most sacred bond of benefits from which friendship springs. 18.6 "It is not always permitted me," he says, "to say, 'I am unwilling'; sometimes a benefit must be received even against one's will. A cruel and irascible tyrant gives, who will count it an injury that you scorn his gift: shall I not receive it? Put in the same case a brigand, a pirate, a king with the spirit of a brigand and a pirate. What shall I do? Is he too unworthy for me to owe him a debt?" 18.7 When I say that you must choose to whom you are to owe, I make exception of superior force and fear, under which all choice perishes. If it is free to you, if it is in your own power to will or not, you will weigh the matter with yourself; if necessity takes away the choice, you will know that you are not receiving, but obeying. No man is laid under obligation by receiving what he was not allowed to refuse; if you wish to know whether I am willing, make it possible for me to be unwilling. "He gave you your life, nonetheless!" 18.8 It matters not what is given, unless it is given by one who is willing, to one who is willing; if you have saved me, you are not therefore my savior. Poison has sometimes served as a remedy; it is not for that reason counted among wholesome things. Some things profit, yet lay no one under obligation. A man who had come to kill a certain tyrant lanced his tumor with his sword; the tyrant did not for that thank him, that by harming he had cured a thing which the hands of physicians had shrunk from. 19.1 You see that there is no great weight in the deed itself, since he does not seem to have given a benefit who helped with an evil intent; for the benefit was chance, the man's was the wrong. We have watched in the amphitheater a lion who, recognizing one of the beast-fighters who had once been his keeper, protected him from the onslaught of the beasts. Is the help of a wild beast, then, a benefit? By no means, since it neither wished to do it nor did it with the intent of doing it. 19.2 Where I have placed the wild beast, place a tyrant; both the one and the other gave life, yet neither the one nor the other gave a benefit. Since it is no benefit to be compelled to receive, it is no benefit to owe to one whom you would not. You must first give me control of myself, then your benefit. 20.1 It is wont to be debated concerning Marcus Brutus, whether he ought to have accepted his life from the deified Julius, when he judged that Julius ought to be slain. 20.2 On what principle he acted in slaying him we shall treat elsewhere; for to me, though he was a great man in other respects, in this matter he seems to have erred grievously and not to have acted by the Stoic teaching. Either he dreaded the name of king, although the best condition of a state is under a just king; or he hoped that liberty would exist there where the reward of both ruling and serving was so great; or he supposed that the state could be recalled to its earlier form, its old morals being lost, and that there would be equality of civil right and that the laws would stand in their place, in a city where he had seen so many thousands of men fighting, not over whether they should be slaves, but over which master they should serve! And how great a forgetfulness of the nature of things or of his own city possessed him, who believed that, when one man was slain, there would not be another to want the same thing, although a Tarquin had been found after so many kings had been cut off by sword and lightning! 20.3 But he ought to have accepted his life, yet not for that reason to have held Caesar in a parent's place, because it was through a wrong that Caesar had come into the right of giving a benefit; for he who has not killed has not saved, nor did he give a benefit, but a reprieve. 21.1 This can come more into some debate: what a captive should do, to whom a man of prostituted body and infamous mouth promises the price of his ransom. Shall I suffer myself to be saved by one so foul? Then, having been saved, what gratitude shall I render him? Shall I live with one so obscene? Shall I not live with my ransomer? I shall tell you what I judge best. 21.2 Even from such a man I shall accept the money I am to pay down for my freedom, but I shall accept it as a loan, not as a benefit; I shall pay him back the money, and, if there is occasion to save him when in peril, I shall save him; into the friendship which joins like to like I shall not descend, nor shall I count him in the place of a savior, but of a moneylender, to whom I know I must repay what I received. 21.3 There is a man worthy enough that I should receive a benefit from him, but it will harm the giver; for this reason I shall not receive it, because he is ready to help me to his own disadvantage or even peril. He means to defend me on a charge, but by that advocacy he will make a king his enemy; I am his enemy, if, when he is willing to risk himself for me, I do not do the easier thing, namely, to face the risk without him. 21.4 Hecaton sets down a silly and frivolous example, that of Arcesilaus, who, he says, did not accept money brought to him by a son of a family, lest the young man should offend his miserly father. What did he do worthy of praise, in that he did not receive stolen goods, in that he preferred not to accept rather than to repay? For what self-restraint is there in not receiving another man's property? 21.5 If we need an example of greatness of soul, let us use that of Julius Graecinus, an excellent man, whom Gaius Caesar killed for this one thing, that he was a better man than it is expedient for anyone to be under a tyrant. When he was receiving from his friends contributions toward the expense of the games, he did not accept a great sum of money sent by Fabius Persicus, and when those who weigh, not the senders, but the things sent, chided him for having refused it: "Shall I," said he, "accept a benefit from a man from whom I would not accept a pledge of the cup?" 21.6 When Rebilus, a man of consular rank and of the same ill repute, had sent him a larger sum and pressed him to order it accepted: "I beg you," he said, "pardon me; I did not accept from Persicus either." Is this to accept gifts, or to enroll a senate? 22.1 When we have judged that a thing should be accepted, let us accept it cheerfully, professing our joy, and let it be plain to the giver, so that he may reap his reward at once; for it is a just cause of gladness to see a friend glad, a juster to have made him so. Let us show, with outpoured feeling, how welcome it has come to us, bearing witness to it not only in his hearing but everywhere. He who receives a benefit gratefully pays the first installment of it. 23.1 There are some who are unwilling to receive except in secret; they shun a witness and a confidant of the benefit; you may know that such men have an evil intent. As the giver should publish his gift only so far as it will delight the one to whom it is given, so to the receiver an assembly should be summoned; what you are ashamed to owe, do not receive. Some give thanks furtively, in a corner and in the ear; 23.2 that is not modesty, but a kind of disavowal; he is ungrateful who renders thanks with the witnesses removed. Some are unwilling that an account should be opened in their name, that brokers be brought in or witnesses summoned to seal, or that they give a written bond. The same thing is done by those who take pains that a benefit conferred on them be as unknown as possible. 23.3 They are afraid to make it public, that they may be said to have attained their ends by their own virtue rather than by another's aid; they are seldom seen rendering service to those to whom they owe their life or their dignity, and, while they fear the reputation of clients, they incur the heavier reputation of the ungrateful. 24.1 Others speak most evilly of those who have deserved best of them. It is safer to give offense to certain men than to oblige them; for they seek, through hatred, a proof that they owe nothing. And yet nothing is more to be insisted on than that the memory of services should cling to us, and this must be refreshed from time to time, because no one can return gratitude save he who remembers, and he who remembers returns it. 24.2 We must receive a benefit neither daintily nor in a cringing and humble fashion; for if a man is careless in receiving, when every benefit is fresh and open before him, what will he do when its first pleasure has cooled? Another receives it disdainfully, like one who says: 24.3 "I have no need of it, to be sure, but since you wish it so strongly, I shall give you power over me"; another receives it indifferently, so as to leave the giver in doubt whether he even noticed it; another barely parts his lips, and was more ungrateful than if he had held his peace. 24.4 One must speak more warmly, in proportion to the greatness of the thing, and add these words: "You have laid more men under obligation than you think" (for everyone rejoices that his benefit reaches further); "you do not know what you have bestowed on me, but you ought to know how much greater it is than you suppose" (he is at once grateful who loads himself with the debt); "I shall never be able to return you gratitude; this at least I shall not cease to confess everywhere, that I cannot return it." 25.1 By nothing did Furnius oblige Caesar Augustus more, and render him more ready to grant other requests, than that, when he had obtained pardon for his father, who had followed the party of Antony, he said: "This one injury, Caesar, I have at your hands: you have brought it about that I both live and die ungrateful." What is so much the mark of a grateful soul as in no way to satisfy itself, as not even to come near the hope of ever equaling the benefit? 25.2 By these and like utterances let us strive that our good will be not hidden, but laid open and shine forth. Though words be wanting, if we are affected as we ought to be, our consciousness of it will stand out upon our face. 25.3 He who means to be grateful, let him think at once, while he is receiving, of repaying. Chrysippus, indeed, says that, like one set in a footrace and shut in the starting-stalls, he ought to await his time, at which, as at a given signal, he may dart forth; and indeed he needs great effort, great speed, to overtake the one ahead. 26.1 We must now see what most makes men ungrateful. It is either an excessive self-regard and that fault implanted in mortality of admiring oneself and one's own, or greed, or envy. 26.2 Let us begin with the first. Everyone is a kindly judge of himself. Hence it comes that he thinks he has deserved everything, and takes it as a payment due, and does not think himself valued at his proper price. "This he gave me, but how late, but after how many toils! How much more I might have attained, if I had chosen to court this man or that, or myself! I had not hoped for this; I have been flung into the crowd. Did he judge me worthy of so little? It had been more honorable to be passed over." 27.1 Gnaeus Lentulus the augur, the greatest example of riches before his freedmen made him poor, this man who saw his four hundred million sesterces (I have spoken exactly; for he did no more than see them), was barren of wit, as petty in mind as he was great in fortune. Though he was most avaricious, he let go of coins more readily than of words: so great was his poverty of speech. 27.2 Though he owed all his advancement to the deified Augustus, to whom he had brought a poverty laboring under the burden of nobility, now the chief man of the state in both money and influence, he used from time to time to complain of Augustus, saying that he had been drawn away from his studies; that not so much had been heaped upon him as he had lost by abandoning eloquence. And yet among other things the deified Augustus had bestowed this too on him, that he had freed him from ridicule and fruitless toil! 27.3 Greed suffers no man to be grateful; for what is given is never enough for a wicked hope, and we crave the more the more has come to us, and avarice is far more inflamed when it is lodged amid a heap of great riches, just as the force of a flame is infinitely keener the greater the conflagration from which it has flashed forth. 27.4 Likewise ambition suffers no man to rest content in that measure of honors which once was his shameless prayer. No one renders thanks for a tribuneship, but complains that he has not been carried all the way to the praetorship; nor is this welcome, if the consulship is lacking; not even this satisfies, if it is but one. Desire reaches out beyond itself, and does not understand its own good fortune, because it looks back, not at whence it has come, but at whither it tends. 28.1 More violent and more troublesome than all these is the evil of envy, which disquiets us while it compares: "This he bestowed on me, but on that man more, but on that man sooner"; and then it pleads no one's cause, but is partial to itself against all. How much simpler, how much wiser to magnify the benefit received, to know that no one is valued by another so highly as by himself! 28.2 "I ought to have received more, but it was not easy for him to give more; his liberality had to be divided among many; this is a beginning, let us take it in good part, and by gratefully receiving call forth his spirit; he did little, but he will do it oftener; he preferred that man to me, but me to many; that man is not my equal in virtues or in services, but he had his own charm; by complaining I shall not make myself worthy of greater gifts, but unworthy of those given. More has been given to those most base men; what of it? How rarely does fortune use judgment! Daily we complain that the wicked are prosperous; 28.3 often the hail that has passed over the little fields of every worst man has smitten the crop of the best men; each man bears his own lot, as in other matters so in friendships." 28.4 No benefit is so full that malice cannot carp at it, none so meager that a good interpreter cannot enlarge it. Causes for complaint will never be lacking, if you look at benefits from their worse side. 29.1 See how unjust are the appraisers of the divine gifts, and these the very men who profess wisdom. They complain that we do not equal elephants in size of body, deer in swiftness, birds in lightness, bulls in onset; that the hide of beasts is solid, that of fallow deer more comely, that of bears thicker, that of beavers softer; that dogs surpass us in keenness of scent, eagles in sharpness of sight, ravens in length of years, many creatures in ease of swimming. 29.2 And although nature does not allow certain things even to meet in the same subject, such as swiftness of body and strength, they call it an injury that man is not compounded of diverse and discordant goods, and they call the gods careless of us, because good health, unconquerable even by our vices, was not given us, because foreknowledge of the future was not. They scarcely refrain from carrying themselves to such a pitch of impudence as to hate Nature, because we are below the gods, because we do not stand on a level with them. 29.3 How much better to return to the contemplation of so many and so great benefits, and to give thanks that they have willed us to draw the second lot in this most beautiful dwelling place, that they have set us over the things of earth! Does anyone compare with us those animals whose mastery lies in our hands? Whatever has been denied us could not have been given. 29.4 Therefore, whoever you are, unjust appraiser of the human lot, consider how much our parent has bestowed on us, how much stronger animals we have sent beneath the yoke, how much swifter ones we overtake, how nothing mortal is placed beyond the reach of our blow. 29.5 So many virtues we have received, so many arts, the mind, in fine, to which nothing is not penetrable in the same instant in which it directs itself, swifter than the stars, whose future courses, after many ages, it outruns; then such abundance of crops, such abundance of wealth, such a heaping of things upon things. You may go round all creation and, because you will find nothing whole that you would rather be, may pick out single things from all that you would wish given to you; when Nature's indulgence is rightly weighed, you must confess that you have been her darling.
